p: At the Capitol Henry found four steps marked one mile high, each one true in the year somebody set it. Check the year.
At Meridian, everything that checks anything reports to the finance chief, Carla Wynn, and internal audit hasn't met the board's audit committee in two years.
The daily reconciliation against the Federal Reserve caught differences on March 3 and March 4. Both were waved off as timing, by someone who signed B.N.
Leonard asked him to soften the finding. Henry kept it, and offered to put Leonard's own emails beside it.
Meridian's chairman, Simon Kade, wants to meet him. And Laura wants coffee on Monday, to ask him something in person.
Simon Kade. Meridian's founder, chairman and chief executive. Charming, and very glad to meet Henry.
Nkechi Obi. The FBI agent. She rings when she wants something, and says so.
Laura. Maisie's mother. In eight years she's never asked Henry for anything in person.
Precious Mensah. The night nurse at Elmcroft, his father's care home.
Maisie Ashby. Henry's daughter, on spring break.

The clocks had gone forward early on Sunday, and Henry had spent the lost hour the way he spent most of his hours now, at the desk on Wazee Street with the radiator knocking. On Monday morning London was six hours ahead instead of seven. It felt like a small favor from somebody who didn't know him.
Giles had written at 6:12, which was lunchtime at One Lime Street.

An email from Giles Fenwick. Subject: The board. Board read your interim view aloud, start to finish. Reserve stands. No decision on payment until your report. Their chairman rang ours at home on Saturday to say how much he's looking forward to meeting you. Ours didn't enjoy it. G.

Their chairman was Simon Kade, who was also their chief executive, and whose assistant had written on Saturday morning, through counsel this time, offering lunch at Meridian on Monday at half past twelve. Vellacott's counsel had said yes on his behalf, with rules. Meridian's general counsel would be there, and so would she. It was a courtesy. Nobody would discuss findings.

He looked Kade up while the kettle boiled. Meridian's website had a photograph of a tall man in an open collar, laughing at something just out of frame, and a paragraph about trust and speed that didn't say where he'd been before Meridian. He noticed it the way you notice a stair that isn't there.
Somebody else is doing the work.

Every company you audit will tell you that some piece of the work belongs to somebody else, Lime Street. The payroll's with a provider. The servers are in somebody's cloud. The settlement files get handled by a firm across town. Fine. People outsource for good reasons: skills they don't have, cost, scale. What they can't outsource is the accountability. If the vendor loses the data, the company lost it. Write that on your hand.

So vendor management is a life cycle, and you audit each stage of it. Before the contract: why outsource at all, and is this vendor fit to do it? Due diligence means looking at the vendor's finances, its controls, its people, its own suppliers, and who owns it. Who owns it matters more than people think. A vendor that belongs to one of your directors is a related party. That contract should be disclosed and approved by people with no interest in it.

The contract is where the company keeps its rights, so read it the way you'd read a will. What's the service, and how is it measured? Service levels, with numbers. Is there a right to audit, or at least a promise of independent assurance, such as a SOC 2 Type 2 report? Then confidentiality, limits on how the vendor may use the data, a duty to report security incidents within a set time, rules for subcontracting, and the way out: how the data comes back or gets destroyed when it ends. For software the company can't live without, look for source code escrow.

Then monitoring, for as long as the contract runs. Somebody owns the relationship, reviews performance against the service levels, reads the assurance reports, and chases the exceptions. A service level report the vendor writes about itself is the vendor's opinion. Check it against the company's own records. And match the effort to the risk. The coffee machine people need a contract. A firm with administrator access to production needs everything above.

How the exam asks it. Outsourcing moves the work, never the accountability. For a vendor that handles critical systems or sensitive data, the contract term the exam cares most about is the right to audit, or an agreed independent assurance report. Monitoring compares actual performance with the SLA, using evidence the vendor didn't write.
People and money are resources too.

IT resource management is a dull name for how a company decides who does the work, what it costs, and what happens when somebody leaves. Start with people. Anyone in a sensitive job, employee or contractor, gets screened before they start. They have a job description that says what they may and may not do. When they go, their access goes the same day, and somebody checks that it went.

Then two controls that look like kindness and aren't. Mandatory leave means everyone in a sensitive job is away from it for a stretch, usually two weeks in a row, every year, while somebody else does the work. Job rotation moves people between duties on a schedule. They work for the same reason. Most fraud needs its author in the chair every day, answering the questions and keeping the story straight. Take them out of the chair and the story has to stand up without them. Bank examiners have pushed for it for longer than you've been alive. When somebody tells me proudly that nobody on the team has taken a holiday in years, I don't hear loyalty. I hear a control that isn't running.

Watch for key person dependency, where one person is the only one who knows how a system works. Cross training, written procedures, and a succession plan are the controls. The same risk turns up inside vendors, where the one person who understands your system works for somebody else.

Sourcing is a resource decision as well. In house, outsourced, or a mix should come out of a business case that weighs cost, skills, risk, and control. And the company should keep enough expertise of its own to manage the vendor, because a company that can't tell good work from bad can't manage anybody. Then the money: an IT budget tied to the strategy, actual spending compared with it, and costs charged back to the parts of the business that use the service, so they can see what it costs.

How the exam asks it. The main purpose of mandatory leave and job rotation is to detect errors and irregularities, because a substitute does the job. When one person holds all the knowledge of a critical system, cross training and documented procedures are the controls to pick.

Data governance answers a question that sounds easy: who's in charge of this data? Every important set of data needs an owner, a named person in the business, usually a senior manager, who's accountable for it. The owner decides how sensitive it is, who may use it, and how long it's kept. IT is usually the custodian. The custodian runs the systems, takes the backups, and applies the controls the owner asks for. Users use it, within the rules. When IT names itself the owner, the people who know what the data is worth have been taken out of the decision, usually without noticing.

Classification is how the owner's judgment becomes controls. A company picks a short scheme, something like public, internal, confidential, and restricted, and says what each label requires: who can see it, whether it's encrypted, whether it may go to a vendor. Then every control keyed to the label inherits whatever mistake went into choosing it. A label set too low is a gate left open with a sign on it that says shut.

You can't classify what you haven't found, so the work starts with an inventory: what data the company holds, where every copy lives, including the copies at vendors, and who owns each one. Then the life cycle. Data gets created, used, shared, archived, and finally destroyed, under a retention schedule that meets the law and the business's needs and goes no further. Keeping data longer than you need it isn't caution. It's exposure. Data quality belongs here too: whether the data is accurate and complete enough for the decisions people make with it.

How the exam asks it. The data owner classifies data and approves access. The custodian implements the protection. Before anything can be classified, the organization has to know what data it holds, where, and who owns it.

Privacy is about personal information: what a company collects about people, why, what it does with it, and who else gets it. Security is part of privacy. It isn't all of it. A company can keep a file perfectly safe and still be using it for something nobody agreed to.

The principles behind most privacy laws are old and short. Tell people what you collect and why. Give them a choice where they're owed one. Collect only what you need for the purpose you stated, and use it only for that purpose. Keep it accurate. Keep it no longer than you need. Protect it. Let people see and correct what you hold about them. And somebody is answerable for all of it.

A privacy program puts those principles to work. There's a person responsible, often called a privacy officer. There's a notice that tells people the truth. There's a map of the personal data and where it flows. And there's a privacy impact assessment before any new system, process, or vendor starts handling personal data, so the risks get dealt with in the design instead of in the apology.

Here's where the vendor comes back in. When a company tells its customers their data goes only to providers bound by contract to protect it, the contracts had better say so. In the United States, the Gramm Leach Bliley Act makes financial institutions protect their customers' nonpublic personal information, and the rules under it expect them to choose providers who can safeguard it, require the safeguards by contract, and check on them from time to time. A promise in a notice that never made it into a contract is a promise nobody kept.
And you handle personal data too, every time you test. Take only the fields your test needs. Mask what you can. Keep it safe while you have it, and get rid of it when the work allows.

How the exam asks it. A privacy impact assessment is done before personal data is processed in a new way, ideally at design. A privacy notice is a commitment, so test whether contracts and practices actually deliver it.

Quality assurance and quality control get used as if they meant the same thing. They don't. Quality control checks the product: this release, this report, this file. Quality assurance checks the process that makes the product, so good results come out by design instead of by luck. Both need some distance from the work. A QA team that reports to the manager whose work it tests will be asked, now and then, to be reasonable.

Plenty of companies run a quality management system against a standard, most often ISO 9001. An independent certification body audits it and, if it's satisfied, issues a certificate. That means something. But only within its scope, which is written on the certificate in one line most people never read. A certificate for customer support says nothing about the payment engine. Read the scope, read the dates, and if you need more, ask for the certification audit report.

Other models rate how mature a company's processes are, CMMI being the one you'll hear most, from ad hoc at the bottom to measured and continually improved at the top. Whatever the model, I look for the same things. Quality requirements written down and measurable. Reviews and tests before release, not after a customer complains. Defects traced to their causes, and the causes fixed. And vendors' work held to the same standard as the company's own. A company that tests its own code with care and takes a vendor's code on the vendor's word has half a quality system.

How the exam asks it. QA is about the process and QC about the product. QA should be independent of the people whose work it reviews. When an answer leans on a certificate, check that its scope covers the area in question.

Enterprise architecture is a company's map of itself: its business processes, the applications that support them, the data that moves between them, and the technology underneath. A good one has two drawings. The current state is what exists today. The target state is where the company has decided to go. The gap analysis between them becomes the plan, and somebody, usually an architecture review board, decides which projects close which gaps and checks that new work fits.

There are frameworks for drawing it. The Zachman Framework is a grid: what, how, where, who, when, and why, asked from each point of view, from the planner's down to the builder's. TOGAF, from The Open Group, works across four domains, business, data, application, and technology, with a method for getting from the current state to the target. You don't need to draw either. You need to know what they're for.

I use architecture to find things. The map shows every system, every interface, and every door to the outside, and your job is to check the map against the ground. Lay the documented connections beside the access lists and the network rules. Anything on the ground that isn't on the map is either a mistake in the drawing or something nobody wanted drawn. Either way it's a finding.

Then compare the target with what happened. A target state approved years ago and never reached is a decision made by default, by whoever didn't do the work. Ask who accepted the gap. Usually nobody did. That's the finding too.

How the exam asks it. Gap analysis compares the current state with the target state. Enterprise architecture should support business strategy and give an accurate, current picture of systems, data flows, and interfaces, including third party connections.

At eight he read through his own disclosure note from Tuesday, the one that had sent Meridian's lawyers away on Friday in four minutes. It was dull, and dated, and it said exactly what he'd known and when. He'd never been so fond of a dull document.

At 8:10 counsel rang. The Federal Reserve totals for March 2 to 5 wouldn't come today. Meridian's bank wanted the request signed by Meridian itself, and Meridian's general counsel was "reviewing the form." Henry wrote the delay in the file with the date and who had caused it, because a delay is evidence too. Then he sent Giles two lines, since the interim view had promised him the totals today: they'd slipped, and here was why.

At 8:40 he went through Meridian's answer to a request he'd made on Wednesday: every outside company that touched the settlement service, with its contract. There were fourteen. Most sold Meridian the things any office buys, a phone system, a payroll service, the coffee machines. Five had access to production. He read their rows from the bottom up.

Meridian Clearing, vendor register (extract, production access). Pellridge Data Services, Inc., Denver. Service: settlement operations support and file archive. Access: production, administrator, settlement release service. Contract: July 2019, signed for Meridian by C. Wynn, CFO. Renews yearly. Right to audit: none. Independent assurance report: none on file. Last vendor review: none recorded. Related party: No. Other vendors with production access (4): right to audit, yes. SOC 2 Type 2 on file, yes.
Four rows that looked the way rows should, and one that didn't.
Pellridge's register row says none three times. What should Henry do about it?
A. Tell Giles that Pellridge's access is how the intruder got in.
B. Note that Meridian shows no oversight of a vendor with admin access.
C. Ask counsel for a SOC 2 report from Pellridge to match the other four.
D. Ring Pellridge and ask them to send their controls documents today.

He writes it as a condition: a vendor with administrator access to the settlement release service, no right to audit, no independent assurance, and no review since 2019. Under it he writes the criteria the way Dot would have. The company that outsources a service keeps the accountability for it. Then he asks counsel for Pellridge's due diligence file from 2019, and for anything at all showing that someone at Meridian ever checked Pellridge's work.

Tick, agreed to source. Outsourcing moves the work, not the accountability. Meridian should have done due diligence before signing, kept a right to audit or obtained independent assurance, and monitored the vendor in proportion to its access. Record what's missing, then ask for whatever would prove you wrong.
At twenty past ten he opened the claim pack to page 44, where Meridian had drawn its settlement architecture for the insurer: tidy boxes, arrows, a legend in the corner.

Settlement architecture, current state (claim pack, page 44). Merchant portal, to settlement application, to release gateway (dual authorization), to the Federal Reserve. Monitoring: DOME, all components. Third party connections: shown at the edge of each component.

He laid the vendor register beside it. Four of the five vendors with production access were drawn in, as small gray boxes at the edges. Pellridge, with administrator access to the release service, wasn't on the page at all.
How should Henry use Meridian's architecture diagram from page 44?
A. Check the drawing against the access list and log each missing link.
B. Take the diagram as given and use it to scope the testing.
C. Sketch his own map of the real environment and work from that instead.
D. Ask Leonard for an updated diagram showing all vendor links.

He does it line by line, every vendor with production access against every connection on page 44. Pellridge is the only one missing. He writes the condition and the source of each half, then asks counsel for Meridian's interface inventory and its architecture documents, current and planned, with their approval dates. If the drawing and the list disagree, one of them is wrong, and the company ought to know which.

That's the one, Lime Street. Enterprise architecture should give an accurate picture of systems, data flows, interfaces, and third party connections. Testing the documented architecture against an independent inventory finds what's missing, and an undocumented connection into production is a finding in itself.
Decision three. Lit like a painting.

Meridian had the top two floors of a glass tower on Seventeenth Street. At 12:25 Henry stood in the lobby with Vellacott's counsel, who'd come to make sure lunch stayed lunch, and looked at the wall behind the reception desk. It held one framed certificate, lit like a painting.

Certificate of registration, Meridian Clearing reception. ISO 9001:2015. Meridian Clearing, Inc. Quality management system. Scope: merchant onboarding and customer support services. Valid until June 2028.
The receptionist saw him reading it. Mr. Kade's very proud of that one, she said.
Meridian's lobby has an ISO 9001 certificate lit like a painting. What should Henry make of it?
A. Read the scope line printed on the certificate first.
B. Dismiss the certificate as marketing for the lobby wall.
C. Ask for the certification body's latest audit report first.
D. Record the certificate as evidence of quality in settlement.

He copies the scope into his notebook word for word. The certificate is real, and probably earned. It covers onboarding and customer support, the parts of Meridian that face its customers, and stops well short of the part that moves the money. He'll ask counsel for the latest certification audit report to see what was looked at, but he already knows what wasn't.

Good. Write it down. Certification is only as wide as its scope. Read the scope statement and the dates, and if you need more, ask for the certification body's audit report. A quality certificate for one process says nothing about another.

Simon Kade came down to collect them himself, which chairmen don't usually do. He was tall and easy, with a good handshake and a better memory. He'd read up on Henry, or had somebody do it for him, and he asked about the Intelligence Corps as if it were a school they'd both nearly gone to.

I was sorry about Dorothy Kessler, he said in the lift, before anyone else could say anything. She examined us for nine years. Terrifying woman. I liked her enormously. Henry said thank you, and felt Vellacott's counsel not look at him.
She had a name for everyone, did you know? Nine years, and I was never once Simon. I was the Chairman, said like a diagnosis. He smiled as if they had that in common. I expect she had one for you.
Henry watched the floor numbers climb and didn't tell him. It was the one thing of hers nobody had put in an evidence bag.
Lunch was in a corner room with the whole Front Range in the window. Meridian's general counsel sat at the end of the table and wrote things down. Kade ate almost nothing and talked well.

Here's the secret of this company, Mr. Ashby. We're small. Eleven people run settlement for more banks than you'd believe. In 2019 we handed the machinery to Pellridge, good people, old friends, and IT went from sixteen to five. And my settlement team? Nobody's taken a full week off since 2019. They won't. I've tried to make them. He smiled. You can't buy that kind of loyalty.
Kade calls his team's habit loyalty. How should Henry respond?
A. Tell Kade that loyalty like that is worth a great deal.
B. Ask Kade which of his team approve the settlement files.
C. Explain to Kade that banks expect two weeks' leave, and why.
D. Note the remark and ask counsel for leave records.

He nods and lets Kade talk. Under the table, in his notebook, he writes: No enforced absence in settlement roles since 2019 (CEO, verbal). IT outsourced to Pellridge 2019, staff 16 to 5 (CEO, verbal). Request leave records, job descriptions, staffing plan, through counsel. Kade's words are inquiry, the weakest evidence there is. They're also an excellent map of where to look.

Tick, agreed to source. Mandatory leave and job rotation are old banking controls, because most fraud needs its author in the chair every day. A small team that never steps away and relies on a vendor's staff is a resource management risk. Treat the remark as inquiry and confirm it with records.
Over coffee Kade leaned back in his chair.

Here's what I'd like to do. You're getting what you need from my lawyers a teaspoon at a time, and I'm sorry about that. So I'll have the team put our whole customer file on a drive for you this afternoon. Every merchant, every account, every cardholder. The lot. Then you've got everything. He turned his cup on its saucer. And in return, just tell me what you've found so far. If something's broken, I'd rather my board heard it from me on Thursday than from anyone else.
Meridian's general counsel studied the ceiling.
Kade offers Meridian's whole customer file in exchange for Henry's findings so far. What should Henry say?
A. Say counsel will ask for just the fields he needs and London gets his results.
B. Decline both and offer to brief Meridian's board himself on Thursday.
C. Say he'll take the drive and sort out which records he needs later.
D. Tell Kade about the Pellridge contract before his board meets Thursday.

That's kind, Henry says. Counsel will send the list of fields I need. Names and card numbers won't be on it. And what I've found so far goes to London first, I'm afraid. Kade laughs as if he'd been beaten fairly at something. Ah, well. Worth a try. The general counsel stops studying the ceiling.

That's the one, Lime Street. Data minimization means taking only the personal data a purpose needs, and an auditor is bound by it like anyone else. And findings go to the client through the agreed channel, never to the auditee's chief executive over coffee.
Decision six. The label decides the gate.
Agent Obi rang at five past three. The bureau had the claim file now, she said, and then she asked what she'd actually rung about. Did he mention her?
He said he liked her enormously.
She let that go. Your father was at Lloyd's too.
He looked at the window for a while. No.
I'm sorry, she said, and sounded it, and rang off.
He hadn't told her about his father. He thought about ringing back to ask how she knew, and opened the classification register instead.

Data classification register (extract). Settlement files: INTERNAL. Merchant bank account details: INTERNAL. Data owner: CIO. Classified: 2019, by IT. Next review: 2020. From the classification standard: RESTRICTED data may go to a vendor only with the data owner's written approval and encryption. INTERNAL data may go to any approved vendor.
So the label decided the gate.
Settlement files are labeled Internal, which lets them go to any approved vendor. What should Henry make of that?
A. Accept the labels and test the vendor gate as it was written.
B. Reclassify the settlement files as Restricted in his workpapers.
C. Note that IT set the labels and the low label skipped owner sign off.
D. Ask the CIO to confirm in writing that each of the labels is correct.

The chain runs in order. The CIO's team, the custodian, set the labels in 2019 and named itself owner. Settlement files went down as Internal. Internal data can go to any approved vendor without the owner's sign off, so Pellridge never needed anyone's sign off. Nobody in settlement operations ever chose that risk. He adds a request for whoever in the business should have owned the data.

Good. Write it down. Data owners in the business classify data and approve access to it. Custodians in IT protect it as the owner directs. When the custodian classifies, the label tends to follow convenience, and every control keyed to the label inherits the mistake.

The coffee place on Pearl Street was next door to the bookshop, and at seven on a Monday in spring break it held students, a man with a guitar case, and Laura, at a table by the window with two cups. She'd already bought his. It was the right one. He let that be.
She's put the poster on her bedroom door, she said. With the error in the corner. She tells people it's a real analysis.

Here's the ask. My husband's father is having surgery in Duluth the week of my defense. It was booked before my date was set, and he has to go. So I need you to have Maisie from Monday the twenty ninth to Thursday the first. School run included. That's Denver to Boulder by eight, and back for her at three thirty, four days. She turned her cup a quarter turn. I don't want a yes. I want a true answer.
He opened his mouth and she held up a hand.

Before you answer. I'm going to say this once. When you were in the Army I was married to a man who noticed everything and told me nothing. In 2014 I found a hospital wristband in your kit bag. A field hospital. Your name on it, and a date, and it was the week you rang and said everything was boring. She didn't look away. I never asked. You never said. I put it back in the pocket and I washed the bag. I'm not asking now. I'm telling you what it was like. And I've been the one in the middle, between you and her, for eight years. I'd like to stop. She let that sit. If it's a no, say no. Don't say yes and go quiet. I can plan around no.
He remembered the week. He'd never once thought about the bag. I didn't know you'd found it, he said.
I know. She turned the cup back the other way. That was the whole problem.

Then he looked at the case in his head the way he'd look at a schedule, because she'd asked for a true answer and that was where it was. The week of the twenty ninth would be the end of it, one way or another.
Laura asks Henry to take Maisie for four days, school runs included. What should he say?
A. Ask whether her husband could fly back midweek for the runs.
B. Say yes, then tell her what could go wrong and what he'd do.
C. Say yes straight away and work out the details later.
D. Say probably and promise to confirm once the case settles.

Yes. And here's what could go wrong. That's probably the last week of this case. My phone will ring at odd hours, and London may want me at six in the morning. So tonight I'll tell Giles I'm not available before nine or after three that week, and he can plan round it. Every school run is mine. If anything threatens one, you'll hear it from me by eight the night before, with a fix. She turns over the page in front of her, the running order for her defense with the committee's names down the side, and writes it on the back, all of it, including the eight. Then she folds it into her coat pocket the way you'd keep a receipt. Okay, she says.

Tick, agreed to source. An honest commitment of resources starts from real capacity: what's already booked, what could pull you away, and the backup if it does. Telling the people who'll compete for your time, early, is what makes the promise one you can keep.

At 7:52 on Tuesday morning his phone buzzed. mum says im at yours the week of the 29th. do you have a toaster He looked at his kitchen. He wrote back I will by then, and she sent a thumbs up. He took it.
At half past eight he did something nobody had asked him to do, and looked Pellridge up in the Colorado Secretary of State's business records, which anyone can search for free.

Henry's notes: public business filings. Pellridge Data Services, Inc. Formed 2019. Registered agent: a law office suite on Seventeenth Street. Same registered agent, same suite: 31 entities. One of them: a holding company whose filings name its member as a Kade family trust.

Registered agents serve dozens of companies, sometimes hundreds. It's a business. He knew that. He also knew Meridian's vendor register had a column headed Related party. Over lunch Kade had called them good people, old friends. The register said No.
Pellridge shares a registered agent with a company owned by a Kade family trust. How should Henry handle it?
A. Ask Leonard whether internal audit ever checked Pellridge's owners.
B. Drop it as one of thirty one companies that share an agent.
C. Tell Giles that Kade owns Pellridge and that the register is wrong.
D. Log a possible undisclosed related party and test it via counsel.

He writes it carefully: shared registered agent; register says not related; ownership not established. Then the tests, through counsel. Meridian's related party disclosures. The directors' conflict of interest declarations. Who approved the 2019 contract, and on what due diligence. Pellridge's owners, as Meridian recorded them when it took Pellridge on. If the answer's innocent, those papers will show it. If it isn't, they'll show that too.

That's the one, Lime Street. Vendor due diligence covers who you're contracting with, including conflicts of interest and related parties, which need disclosure and independent approval. A shared agent justifies further testing. It doesn't justify a conclusion.

He'd had the Pellridge contract since Monday morning and hadn't read past the signature block. At ten to ten he read all nine pages, then pulled up Meridian's privacy notice from its own website, the one every merchant agreed to when it signed up.

Meridian privacy notice (website, extract), and Henry's notes on the Pellridge agreement. Notice: "We share your information only with service providers who are bound by contract to keep it confidential and to use it only to provide services to us." Pellridge master services agreement, July 2019: services, service levels, fees, term, renewal, limitation of liability. Confidentiality: not addressed. Use of data: not addressed. Notice of security incidents: not addressed.
He looked for a privacy impact assessment from 2019, when Pellridge started handling merchants' bank details. Meridian's privacy file held nothing for that year.
Meridian's published privacy policy and the Pellridge agreement say different things about data. What should Henry do?
A. Ask Meridian's privacy officer how Pellridge got approved.
B. Conclude Meridian broke federal privacy law and say so in the report.
C. Log the gap between the notice's promise and the contract's terms.
D. Recommend a new privacy addendum with Pellridge straight away.

The finding comes in three parts. Meridian told merchants their data would go only to providers bound by contract to keep it confidential and use it only for Meridian. The contract that sent their bank details to Pellridge says neither. No privacy impact assessment was done before it started. Then a fourth line, for the claim: nothing obliged Pellridge to tell Meridian about a security incident, or when.

Good. Write it down. A privacy program makes sure the organization does what its notice promises. That includes flowing privacy and security terms into vendor contracts and assessing privacy impact before personal data moves to a new party. A missing incident notice clause also matters for any claim's timeline.
Pellridge's invoices came next, a year of them. One line repeated every month: Settlement file archive, seven year retention: $8,400.
Meridian data inventory: settlement files. Locations: settlement application database; release gateway logs; DOME. Retention: seven years, Meridian systems. Disposal: Records team.
Pellridge wasn't on it. By the look of the invoices, a copy of every settlement file Meridian had sent since 2019 was sitting somewhere that Meridian's own inventory didn't know existed.
Pellridge's monthly invoices list a seven year archive. How should Henry treat it?
A. Ask Pellridge directly to send him the archive to compare.
B. Ask counsel to add the Pellridge archive to his data requests.
C. Log a copy of settlement data outside the inventory.
D. Leave the archive alone as an ordinary backup of the files.

He writes it plainly: a copy of settlement data held by a third party since 2019, missing from the data inventory, with no contract terms on retention, return, or destruction, and no owner who knew. Then he rings counsel, because a copy nobody listed is also a copy nobody has preserved. She says she'll write to the bureau before lunch.

Tick, agreed to source. Data governance covers data through its whole life, wherever it sits: inventory, ownership, retention, and disposal, including copies held by vendors. Data that isn't in the inventory is outside every control that depends on it.
Meridian's quality assurance charter arrived just after noon: two pages, and an organization chart with one box on it that mattered.

IT Quality Assurance, charter and reporting line (extract). Staff: 2. Reports to: Head of Settlement Development. Scope: release testing of the settlement application. Vendor releases (Pellridge): accepted on the vendor's own test evidence.
He set it beside the vendor register and read the last line again.
What should Henry conclude from Meridian's IT quality assurance charter?
A. Ask QA for its defect statistics for the last two years.
B. Note that QA reports to the builders and skips vendor releases.
C. Recommend Meridian extend its ISO 9001 certificate to settlement.
D. Accept the charter and note that a QA function exists on paper.

Two lines go in the file. QA reports to the head of the team whose releases it tests. And QA doesn't test Pellridge's releases at all. It takes Pellridge's word for them. Then a third, smaller: the ISO certificate in the lobby stopped at customer support, so nothing outside the company had looked at this either.

That's the one, Lime Street. Quality assurance needs independence from the work it reviews, and its coverage should include work done by vendors. A QA team inside development, which accepts a vendor's own test evidence, gives assurance over half the system at best.
At a quarter past one the architecture documents from his first request list came through counsel. The target architecture was older than the current one, which was the first thing wrong with it.

Settlement target architecture, approved by the Architecture Review Board, October 2019. "By Q4 2020, all third party connections to production will terminate at the integration gateway. No vendor will have direct access to the settlement release service." Architecture Review Board minutes: last meeting held February 2020.
Meridian's target architecture says vendors will connect through a gateway by late 2020. What should Henry do?
A. Ask the CIO when the move to the gateway will be finished.
B. Sketch a new target architecture and send it to the CIO and the board.
C. Treat the target as the current state the board approved.
D. Compare the target with today's design and find who accepted the gap.

He sets the two side by side. In October 2019 Meridian decided no vendor would reach the release service directly after 2020. In March 2027 one vendor does, with administrator rights. The board that was meant to watch the plan stopped meeting four months after approving it. He looks for anyone who ever decided to keep the direct connection. There's nobody. He writes that down too, because nobody is an answer.

Good. Write it down. Comparing current state with the approved target shows where the plan stalled. A gap nobody accepted is a decision made by default, and an architecture review board that stopped meeting is a governance failure in itself.

Giles had answered his email from the night before at 6:02 that morning. Diary blocked, 29 March to 1 April, nothing before 9 or after 3 your time. Didn't know you had it in you. G. Henry had forwarded it to Laura without a word, because it was the kind of thing she'd asked to be told.

At 1:35 counsel rang to say Meridian had acknowledged the Pellridge requests and would respond "in due course." Nobody at Meridian had asked why he wanted them. As far as he could tell, nobody at Meridian knew.

Every finding from the two days came back to the same door. A company nobody at Meridian had checked had held the keys to the release service since 2019, and in all that time the only person who'd looked up who owned it was him, this morning, for free.
At two his phone showed the Elmcroft number. It was eight in the evening in Muswell Hill, six hours away now instead of seven, and the call felt early, though it was exactly on time.

He's asleep already, Henry. Long day. The hairdresser came, and he told her all about the Room. A pause, and a page turning. I went through the visitors' book, because of what he said last week. This year's, and last year's as well, to be sure. There's no Dorothy in either. No Kessler. Nobody from America at all.
He wrote it down. Whatever his father knew about an American with a red folder, he hadn't learned it at Elmcroft.
One other thing. It's not about the book. She said it the way nurses say things they've already decided to say. He asked for you at tea. I told him you were in America. He said, 'Still?'
Henry wrote that down too, out of habit, with the time beside it: 2:06 PM. Then he looked at it for a while, and drew a line through the time.
